average_length.about: Measured from a session's first activity to its last, where activity is a page opening or any input, including pointer moves. Time a tab stays open afterward doesn't count. The session list shows each recording's full length, from its start to its last event.

coverage.title: What AgentCake records
coverage.lead: AgentCake classifies each session on this computer, when new activity arrives and again when the session goes inactive. It doesn't call any AI service.

rows.how: There are no automation traces and no agent name, and the behavior model judges the actions to be human.

rows.what: A browser extension, an AI browser, or a cloud agent, like Claude in Chrome, Comet, or ChatGPT agent
rows.shown_as: Agent, named when the evidence identifies it
rows.how: There are agent traces in the page or the browser, and the behavior model judges the actions to be an agent's. Traces include an extension acting on the page or a cloud computer's fixed setup. The name comes from a verified signature, the product's own traces, or the User-Agent.

rows.what: The built-in browser of an AI desktop app, or a cloud agent that gives its name
rows.shown_as: Agent, identified by name, such as Codex browser
rows.how: The User-Agent contains a name, or a verified signature names the visitor. The behavior model still splits the session into stretches.

rows.what: An automated browser that doesn't give its name, like Playwright, Puppeteer, or Selenium
rows.shown_as: Agent, identified by the tool's name when its traces show it, otherwise Unnamed
rows.how: The browser shows automation markers, such as webdriver, a headless browser, or requests without a language header. The behavior model splits the session into stretches. Crawler-like patterns only go into the reasons.

rows.what: A program that gives its name and isn't an agent: a search engine, a monitor, a link preview
rows.shown_as: Counted only; “Verified” when a signature or the operator's published address range confirms it
rows.how: The User-Agent or a signature matches the list of programs that aren't agents. It's marked “Verified” when a published address range or a signature confirms it. The behavior model doesn't run.

rows.what: A human and an agent taking turns
rows.shown_as: Human + agent, split at each hand-off
rows.how: The behavior model finds both a human and an agent in the same session and marks the hand-off where the actions change.

rows.what: Too few actions, or a phone or tablet
rows.shown_as: Human, marked Thin evidence, with the reason
rows.how: There are fewer actions than the behavior model needs, or the visit comes from a phone or tablet, so no guess is made. A setting controls how many actions the model needs.

rows.what: Evidence that's too weak or points both ways
rows.shown_as: Human, marked Thin evidence, with the reason
rows.how: The evidence is too weak or points both ways. Examples include a trace that open DevTools also leave and keyboard navigation like an assistive tool's.

bot.question: What counts as a bot
bot.answer: A bot is a program that names itself and is known to have no human behind it, such as a search engine, a monitor, or a link preview. A visitor that only seems automated counts as an Agent, never a Bot.
